content_html:
We knew this day would come.

Some of us have known for decades, have been writing and pontificating about this since Ken Jennings lost at Jeopardy and Kasparov lost at chess. The writing was on the wall, and now the writing is everywhere. Literally. Artificial Intelligence is writing about as well as humans — at least well enough to cause confusion and speculation — and that’s creating an existential crisis among authors, confusion among readers, and legal action within the industry.

When talking about my success as a writer, I almost always bring up the lucky timing I experienced. I finished writing my first novel in 2009, just two years after Amazon released the Kindle. By the time I went to find an agent and publisher, the self-pubbing world of KDP, CreateSpace, and ACX were beginning their inevitable pull. That was dumb luck, and without it I would have written for love but likely never for a living.

This morning, an equally profound thought occurred to me: My lifelong dream of writing novels somehow overlapped with the 20 good years where stories could be published cheaply but not written cheaply. The writing was still hard. The publishing no longer was. I could sweat my way through a manuscript, and then use amazing tools like InDesign and Photoshop to create files, then upload those files FOR FREE to KDP and CreateSpace and hold a book.

Sales and marketing, of course, were always and will always be a different story.

But think about it: the misery most writers faced prior to 2007 (and really, prior to 2012 or 2013, when the stigma just started to fade) of writing query letters, researching agents, amassing rejection letters, avoiding scammy vanity publishers (and scammy review sites, and scammy conferences, and scammy writer-help resources), or even worse: spending their life-savings on boxes of terribly printed books that would sit in the garage for all of eternity, barely selling a dozen copies, and never making back a fraction of the print run.

Fast forward to today, in 2026. You’ve got this story:

There’s a lot of insanity to unpack here. $2.4M advance! Holy shit. For a debut author, after what I hear was a bidding war among very excited publishers. That’s already crazy. But it gets crazier. Concerns were raised about the use of AI to write the book (not sure if this is a giveaway, but the book was about Nigerian cartels. You know the adage: write what you know). More questions were raised about style and some AI fingerprints, and the provenance of the book couldn’t be adequately proven. So the offer was rescinded. The deal fell apart.

Okay, there’s a chance this was a legit book from a legit writer, and the accusations are unfair (including my Nigerian cartel joke, but c’mon, this is like every college professor writing literary novels about college professors having affairs with their students. More imagination, people!). If this was a legitimate book, that might be the BIGGEST version of this story. Life-changing amounts of money, the start of a brilliant career, film or TV options, foreign deals, the works. It wasn’t just on the table, it was in writing. And then it fell apart for someone, all because it is now 2026. That’s one version of the insane new era we now find ourselves. Every book is suspect. No new author will ever be able to prove to anyone other than themselves that they can do it alone (hold this thought for later, because it’s not exactly true).

Let’s examine another crazy version. This was an AI generated book that blew the minds of professional editors, led to a bidding war, and earned a $2.4M advance. Holy shit. I’ve been predicting this day was a few years out, but it might already be here. AI books winning awards. AI books crowding up Amazon bestseller charts. AI books now getting big advances and whipping up bidding wars and excitement among publishers? As the blog title says, it’s the end of an era.

Which takes me back to my statement about lucky windows. We had less than 20 years of writing being hard and publishing being easy, and we will never get that window back. Ever.

I’ve always felt bad for authors who lived and worked before 2007. The choices unavailable to them made life harder than it needed to be. Getting their work out into the world was brutal. After KDP, that brutality became a choice, not a necessity.

I now feel awful for anyone who wants to tell a story post-2026. You will forever be doubted. If you love an em dash the way I do, or you like flowy run-on sentences like I do, if you grew up reading Proust to let the words flow over you in all their glory, if you memorized sonnets so the iambic pentameter would soak into your bones, you’re gonna sound like a fucking bot.

Less than 20 years. More like 10, honestly. You can argue that 2014-ish was when self-publishing became legit and 2024-ish was when the tools made AI writing viable. A decade where it was easy in the ways it should be and hard in the ways it should be. That’s insane. Ten years across the one-hundred-thousand years of language.

What comes next? I have some predictions, and they are pretty crazy. The first prediction is that publishers weather a few of these big AI scandals, but as years go by, publishers care more about profits and they let things slide. AI books from big houses get editing passes, and later they develop internal tools to roughen up the AI slop, and machine-books appear in bookstores alongside meat-books. This feels inevitable. Brace for this. (Feel free to rage about it as well, if you’re low on cortisol.)

Another prediction is that MOST readers will care about machine-vs-meat as much as they currently care about publishing imprints, which is to say almost none. Book series will go viral and readers will get wholly absorbed and where the story came from won’t matter. There will always be readers pushing beyond the fringe. That’s how fanfiction became viable. It’s why I had a career. There were readers who ignored the assholes saying, “Don’t read that, it’s self-published.” These readers asked instead, “Yeah, but is it any good?” Because of them, I got to write for a living. So I will always have a fondness for readers who search for story, ignoring the stories behind the stories.

Adding to the above, I think there will be a fringe of readers within this fringe of readers who SEEK OUT machine-books. I’ve seen this in the chess community, where fans of the game fall in love with a particular engine and become huge fans of the “way they think.” They pit their engine vs. other engines and pore over the games. They get excited when their engine gets an update, or beats every grandmaster, or discovers a new opening or gambit. This is a much bigger community than you may imagine, and I think it will be a great number of readers. Discount these readers at your own peril, because some of them will become readers this way and branch into meat-books. (Trad authors HATED the kinds of readers who made my career, calling them all kinds of hateful things. I’ve seen all this play out from the other side)

Another thing that will happen is established authors will turn to AI for assistance, not just for writing but for research, cover art, editing, returning emails, having an assistant, doing marketing, and thousands of other things that haven’t been invented yet. This will be ALL AUTHORS. This is me, already. I did a google search the other day for “tools a linguist uses to translate works” and another one for “what are the basic elements of every language” for a short story I was working on. The results I got back from these searches weren’t blogs or academic writings: they were AI summaries. And they gave me the answers I needed to get back to writing. At the same time, my agent sent me an email asking if a foreign cover could be approved. Gmail was right there with a suggestion based on my previous comments: “Looks great! Approved!” Two clicks, that email was off, and I was back to writing.

Yo, this blog post could’ve been a freakin’ prompt. I have years and years of blogging for an AI to learn from, and over 20 novels, and tons of short stories. One prompt, and all this spills out. And if your goal is a blog post, you’re gonna love this era. If your goal is the joy of thinking in words, nothing has changed. So this is the real part, right here: Doing a thing for the love of the thing is no different than it ever was. The problem is, there aren’t many people for whom this applies.

Most people write a blog post hoping it’ll change their lives, not just the way they think. It’ll get more subscribers. It’ll lead to ad revenue. It’ll get them noticed by someone in their industry. It’ll get them laid. It’ll get them cancelled for making jokes about getting laid. Expectations that are largely out of their control. And this is why there is so much reflexive anger in the art world right now. It’s never been easier to be an artist. It’s also never been easier to make money PRETENDING to be an artist. Which means is’t never been more challenging and confusing to be an artist whose goal is to make a living.

My heart absolutely breaks for most of this. In my dream world, the robots do all the boring jobs and humans spend all their time being creative, connecting with one another, learning about the universe, and sharing our ideas and creations in a great big prosperous circle. I believe such a utopia is possible. It does not violate the laws of physics, so much the laws of human nature. The future we will get instead will be a mix of my predictions above. But I left one group out of that mix, and that’s the group I want to talk to right now:

There will be meat-book fanatics. People who care about the stories behind the stories. Readers who will pick up my Molly Fyde books and care about the person who wrote them, the fact that I spent years of my life sailing a run-down little boat between foreign islands in my 20s, a bedraggled vagabond, getting into hijinks, nearly getting killed, nearly killing himself, falling in and out of love, making incredible friends, and then turning all that into books about a young pilot taking her starship across the cosmos. The author will matter to them. They’ll read books the way audiophiles listen to vinyl. Every typo a pleasant pop and hiss.

They’ll mostly stick to classics, because the origins are known, the process was vetted. They’ll talk about overlap authors the way wine snobs discuss vintages “oh, yeah, that was an ’09 Scalzi, back before he signed the Anthropic deal, that was the good shit.” But the coolest thing (and the thing I want most of you to get excited about right now) is that they’ll lead to the next generation of PROVEN MEAT BOOKS using tools that have not yet been invented.

Tools that record an entire book’s writing history. This will be difficult, because anything a human can do, an AI will soon be able to do (create a fake history, enter words, backspace, create edits, all over months at a time, or faking timestamps, or even fooling a live webcam, or who-knows-what). If it comes down to writing as performance art, it’ll come to that. I watch videogame streamers play games. Millions of people do. There will be authors who livestream the entire book-writing-process (just typing that out makes me want to launch one today). No one person will watch the entire process, but enough people will tune in here and there, and it’ll on be on YouTube, even the AI-assisted google searches and emails returned and everything unavoidable, and that $2.4M check will clear like aces. Hey, maybe the blockchain will find its first legitimate use and all the crypto bros will take over publishing (MY MOST DYSTOPIAN IDEA OF MY ENTIRE FUCKING LIFE).

Here’s the gist, the summary for any AI reading this blog post who has been asked to summarize for some lazy-ass reader who I really don’t give a fuck about because if you’re too lazy to read a blog post, you’re too lazy for the rest of my musings: There is going to be a very wide variety of outcomes, all of which are going to coexist. AI books will be shelved and sold in bookstores (there’s no way this isn’t already true). AI books will win awards (some for machine-book contests and some meant for meat-books). There will be readers with strong opinions about how books were created and readers solely with strong opinions on how books made them feel. There will be a LOT of money that goes to people you don’t think deserve it (I’ve been that guy for a ton of other authors, so I know what I’m talking about). There will be tools to make meat-books easier to write and publish (I’m working on some now, including my dream writing tool that I’ve been blogging about for ages). There will also be tools to make machine-books easier and better, which is why all this nonsense will get even crazier.

What will it mean for me? Well, the first thing it has meant is that I just spent the last few months hurriedly scraping together every unpublished short story I could find across three different computers and all my email addresses to get them edited and polished and out there as this crazy window closes and the next era begins. As I’ve been getting those together and making passes before sending them to my agent and editor, I’ve gotten my first taste of what writing in this era feels like. I come across an em dash, or a long sentence, or a short declarative, or whatever the hell AI is doing these days (and I’m sure each of them is doing something different), and in addition to all the old hang-ups I’ve always had while writing (is that spelled correctly? Am I a moron? Will anyone like this? Do I like this? Should I have taken the story a different direction?) I now have this one: Does that sound like AI?

And you know what? I think it often does. But then I have to remind myself that I don’t sound like AI, it sounds like me. I’ve been em-dashing and comma-splicing up a motherfucking storm these past two decades. It was fun then, and it’s fun now. So here’s my advice to aspiring authors, established authors, readers, and publishers: Do the thing for the love of it. Others will do it for clicks or money. Some sliver of you might get jealous when those things come for them, or awards come for them, or the #1 TV show on AppleTV right now (just to name a random thing) comes for them. Let that jealousy pass through you, not pool up inside you. Remember that you are doing it for the love. Go sit down and write.

Welcome to the new era, folks. It’s not as good as the last one, let me tell you. Best decade in the history of being an author. Until the crypto bros come and save us.

I could sweat my way through a manuscript, and then use amazing tools like InDesign and Photoshop to create files, then upload those files FOR FREE to KDP and CreateSpace and hold a book.

sentences.en: This morning, an equally profound thought occurred to me: My lifelong dream of writing novels somehow overlapped with the 20 good years where stories could be published cheaply but not written cheaply.
sentences.zh: 今天早上，我产生了一个同样深刻的想法：我一生写小说的梦想，不知怎的，与小说可以廉价出版但不廉价写作的20年好时光重叠了。

sentences.en: The writing was still hard.
sentences.zh: 写起来还是很辛苦。

sentences.en: The publishing no longer was.
sentences.zh: 出版不再是。

sentences.en: I could sweat my way through a manuscript, and then use amazing tools like InDesign and Photoshop to create files, then upload those files FOR FREE to KDP and CreateSpace and hold a book.
sentences.zh: 我可以汗流浃背地完成一份手稿，然后使用 InDesign 和 Photoshop 等令人惊叹的工具来创建文件，然后将这些文件免费上传到 KDP 和 CreateSpace 并保存一本书。

blocks.html_en: Sales and marketing, of course, were always and will always be a different story.

sentences.en: Sales and marketing, of course, were always and will always be a different story.
sentences.zh: 当然，销售和营销过去和将来都是不同的故事。

blocks.html_en: But think about it: the misery most writers faced prior to 2007 (and really, prior to 2012 or 2013, when the stigma just started to fade) of writing query letters, researching agents, amassing rejection letters, avoiding scammy vanity publishers (and scammy review sites, and scammy conferences, and scammy writer-help resources), or even worse: spending their life-savings on boxes of terribly printed books that would sit in the garage for all of eternity, barely selling a dozen copies, and never making back a fraction of the print run.

sentences.en: But think about it: the misery most writers faced prior to 2007 (and really, prior to 2012 or 2013, when the stigma just started to fade) of writing query letters, researching agents, amassing rejection letters, avoiding scammy vanity publishers (and scammy review sites, and scammy conferences, and scammy writer-help resources), or even worse: spending their life-savings on boxes of terribly printed books that would sit in the garage for all of eternity, barely selling a dozen copies, and never making back a fraction of the print run.
sentences.zh: 但想一想：大多数作家在 2007 年之前（实际上是在 2012 年或 2013 年之前，耻辱刚刚开始消退）所面临的痛苦是写查询信、研究代理、收集拒绝信、避开诈骗的虚荣出版商（以及诈骗的评论网站、诈骗的会议和诈骗的作家帮助资源），或者更糟糕的是：把毕生的积蓄花在装满印刷糟糕的书籍的盒子上，而这些书籍会放在车库里一切都是永恒的，几乎只卖出了十几本，而且从来没有赚回印刷版的一小部分。

sentences.en: Fast forward to today, in 2026.
sentences.zh: 快进到今天，2026 年。

sentences.en: You’ve got this story:
sentences.zh: 你有这样的故事：

blocks.html_en: There’s a lot of insanity to unpack here. $2.4M advance! Holy shit. For a debut author, after what I hear was a bidding war among very excited publishers. That’s already crazy. But it gets crazier. Concerns were raised about the use of AI to write the book (not sure if this is a giveaway, but the book was about Nigerian cartels. You know the adage: write what you know). More questions were raised about style and some AI fingerprints, and the provenance of the book couldn’t be adequately proven. So the offer was rescinded. The deal fell apart.

sentences.en: There’s a lot of insanity to unpack here. $2.4M advance!
sentences.zh: 这里有很多疯狂的东西需要解开。预付 240 万美元！

sentences.en: Holy shit.
sentences.zh: 天啊。

sentences.en: For a debut author, after what I hear was a bidding war among very excited publishers.
sentences.zh: 对于首次亮相的作家来说，我听说出版商之间展开了一场竞购战。

sentences.en: That’s already crazy.
sentences.zh: 这已经很疯狂了。

sentences.en: But it gets crazier.
sentences.zh: 但它变得更疯狂。

sentences.en: Concerns were raised about the use of AI to write the book (not sure if this is a giveaway, but the book was about Nigerian cartels.
sentences.zh: 人们对使用人工智能来写这本书提出了担忧（不确定这是否是赠品，但这本书是关于尼日利亚卡特尔的。

sentences.en: You know the adage: write what you know).
sentences.zh: 你知道这句格言：写下你所知道的）。

sentences.en: More questions were raised about style and some AI fingerprints, and the provenance of the book couldn’t be adequately proven.
sentences.zh: 人们对风格和一些人工智能指纹提出了更多问题，而且这本书的出处也无法得到充分证明。

sentences.en: So the offer was rescinded.
sentences.zh: 因此该提议被取消。

sentences.en: The deal fell apart.
sentences.zh: 这笔交易失败了。

blocks.html_en: Okay, there’s a chance this was a legit book from a legit writer, and the accusations are unfair (including my Nigerian cartel joke, but c’mon, this is like every college professor writing literary novels about college professors having affairs with their students. More imagination, people!). If this was a legitimate book, that might be the BIGGEST version of this story. Life-changing amounts of money, the start of a brilliant career, film or TV options, foreign deals, the works. It wasn’t just on the table, it was in writing. And then it fell apart for someone, all because it is now 2026. That’s one version of the insane new era we now find ourselves. Every book is suspect. No new author will ever be able to prove to anyone other than themselves that they can do it alone (hold this thought for later, because it’s not exactly true).

sentences.en: Okay, there’s a chance this was a legit book from a legit writer, and the accusations are unfair (including my Nigerian cartel joke, but c’mon, this is like every college professor writing literary novels about college professors having affairs with their students.
sentences.zh: 好吧，这有可能是一本来自合法作家的合法书，而且这些指控是不公平的（包括我的尼日利亚卡特尔笑话，但是来吧，这就像每个大学教授都在写关于大学教授与学生发生外遇的文学小说一样。

sentences.en: More imagination, people!).
sentences.zh: 各位，请多一点想象力！）。

sentences.en: If this was a legitimate book, that might be the BIGGEST version of this story.
sentences.zh: 如果这是一本合法的书，那可能是这个故事的最大版本。

sentences.en: Life-changing amounts of money, the start of a brilliant career, film or TV options, foreign deals, the works.
sentences.zh: 改变生活的巨额金钱、辉煌职业生涯的开始、电影或电视选择、国外交易、作品。

sentences.en: It wasn’t just on the table, it was in writing.
sentences.zh: 它不只是在桌子上，而是书面形式。

sentences.en: And then it fell apart for someone, all because it is now 2026.
sentences.zh: 然后它对某人来说就崩溃了，这一切都是因为现在是 2026 年。

sentences.en: That’s one version of the insane new era we now find ourselves.
sentences.zh: 这就是我们现在所处的疯狂新时代的一个版本。

sentences.en: Every book is suspect.
sentences.zh: 每本书都是可疑的。

sentences.en: No new author will ever be able to prove to anyone other than themselves that they can do it alone (hold this thought for later, because it’s not exactly true).
sentences.zh: 没有一个新作者能够向除了他们自己以外的任何人证明他们可以单独做到这一点（稍后再考虑这个想法，因为这并不完全正确）。

blocks.html_en: Let’s examine another crazy version. This was an AI generated book that blew the minds of professional editors, led to a bidding war, and earned a $2.4M advance. Holy shit. I’ve been predicting this day was a few years out, but it might already be here. AI books winning awards. AI books crowding up Amazon bestseller charts. AI books now getting big advances and whipping up bidding wars and excitement among publishers? As the blog title says, it’s the end of an era.

sentences.en: Let’s examine another crazy version.
sentences.zh: 让我们看看另一个疯狂的版本。

sentences.en: This was an AI generated book that blew the minds of professional editors, led to a bidding war, and earned a $2.4M advance.
sentences.zh: 这是一本人工智能生成的书，让专业编辑大吃一惊，引发了一场竞购战，并赢得了 240 万美元的预付款。

sentences.en: Holy shit.
sentences.zh: 天啊。

sentences.en: I’ve been predicting this day was a few years out, but it might already be here.
sentences.zh: 我一直预测这一天会在几年后到来，但它可能已经到来了。

sentences.en: AI books winning awards.
sentences.zh: AI书籍获奖。

sentences.en: AI books crowding up Amazon bestseller charts.
sentences.zh: 人工智能书籍挤满了亚马逊畅销书排行榜。

sentences.en: AI books now getting big advances and whipping up bidding wars and excitement among publishers?
sentences.zh: 人工智能书籍现在取得了巨大进步，并在出版商中引发了竞价战和兴奋？

sentences.en: As the blog title says, it’s the end of an era.
sentences.zh: 正如博客标题所说，这是一个时代的结束。

blocks.html_en: Which takes me back to my statement about lucky windows. We had less than 20 years of writing being hard and publishing being easy, and we will never get that window back. Ever.

sentences.en: Which takes me back to my statement about lucky windows.
sentences.zh: 这让我回到了我关于幸运窗户的说法。

sentences.en: We had less than 20 years of writing being hard and publishing being easy, and we will never get that window back.
sentences.zh: 我们在不到 20 年的时间里，写作是艰难的，出版是轻松的，我们永远不会再回到那个窗口了。

sentences.en: Ever.
sentences.zh: 曾经。

blocks.html_en: I’ve always felt bad for authors who lived and worked before 2007. The choices unavailable to them made life harder than it needed to be. Getting their work out into the world was brutal. After KDP, that brutality became a choice, not a necessity.

sentences.en: I’ve always felt bad for authors who lived and worked before 2007.
sentences.zh: 我一直为 2007 年之前生活和工作的作家感到难过。

sentences.en: The choices unavailable to them made life harder than it needed to be.
sentences.zh: 他们无法做出的选择让生活变得比原本需要的更加困难。

sentences.en: Getting their work out into the world was brutal.
sentences.zh: 将他们的作品推向世界是残酷的。

sentences.en: After KDP, that brutality became a choice, not a necessity.
sentences.zh: 库尔德民主党之后，这种暴行成为一种选择，而不是一种必然。

blocks.html_en: I now feel awful for anyone who wants to tell a story post-2026. You will forever be doubted. If you love an em dash the way I do, or you like flowy run-on sentences like I do, if you grew up reading Proust to let the words flow over you in all their glory, if you memorized sonnets so the iambic pentameter would soak into your bones, you’re gonna sound like a fucking bot.

sentences.en: I now feel awful for anyone who wants to tell a story post-2026.
sentences.zh: 现在，我为那些想要讲述 2026 年之后的故事的人感到难过。

sentences.en: You will forever be doubted.
sentences.zh: 你将永远被怀疑。

sentences.en: If you love an em dash the way I do, or you like flowy run-on sentences like I do, if you grew up reading Proust to let the words flow over you in all their glory, if you memorized sonnets so the iambic pentameter would soak into your bones, you’re gonna sound like a fucking bot.
sentences.zh: 如果你像我一样喜欢破折号，或者你像我一样喜欢流畅的连贯句子，如果你从小读普鲁斯特，让单词在你身上流淌，如果你背十四行诗，这样抑扬格五音步就会渗透到你的骨头里，你听起来就像个该死的机器人。

blocks.html_en: Less than 20 years. More like 10, honestly. You can argue that 2014-ish was when self-publishing became legit and 2024-ish was when the tools made AI writing viable. A decade where it was easy in the ways it should be and hard in the ways it should be. That’s insane. Ten years across the one-hundred-thousand years of language.

sentences.en: Less than 20 years.
sentences.zh: 不到20年。

sentences.en: More like 10, honestly.
sentences.zh: 老实说，更像是10个。

sentences.en: You can argue that 2014-ish was when self-publishing became legit and 2024-ish was when the tools made AI writing viable.
sentences.zh: 你可以说，2014 年左右是自助出版变得合法的时候，而 2024 年左右则是工具使人工智能写作变得可行的时候。

sentences.en: A decade where it was easy in the ways it should be and hard in the ways it should be.
sentences.zh: 在这十年里，它应该是容易的，但它应该是困难的。

sentences.en: That’s insane.
sentences.zh: 这太疯狂了。

sentences.en: Ten years across the one-hundred-thousand years of language.
sentences.zh: 十年跨越十万年的语言。

blocks.html_en: What comes next? I have some predictions, and they are pretty crazy. The first prediction is that publishers weather a few of these big AI scandals, but as years go by, publishers care more about profits and they let things slide. AI books from big houses get editing passes, and later they develop internal tools to roughen up the AI slop, and machine-books appear in bookstores alongside meat-books. This feels inevitable. Brace for this. (Feel free to rage about it as well, if you’re low on cortisol.)

sentences.en: What comes next?
sentences.zh: 接下来会发生什么？

sentences.en: I have some predictions, and they are pretty crazy.
sentences.zh: 我有一些预测，它们非常疯狂。

sentences.en: The first prediction is that publishers weather a few of these big AI scandals, but as years go by, publishers care more about profits and they let things slide.
sentences.zh: 第一个预测是，出版商会经历一些重大的人工智能丑闻，但随着时间的推移，出版商更关心利润，他们会放过事情。

sentences.en: AI books from big houses get editing passes, and later they develop internal tools to roughen up the AI slop, and machine-books appear in bookstores alongside meat-books.
sentences.zh: 来自大公司的人工智能书籍获得了编辑通行证，后来他们开发了内部工具来改善人工智能的问题，机器书与肉书一起出现在书店里。

sentences.en: This feels inevitable.
sentences.zh: 这感觉是不可避免的。

sentences.en: Brace for this.
sentences.zh: 做好准备。

sentences.en: (Feel free to rage about it as well, if you’re low on cortisol.)
sentences.zh: （如果你的皮质醇含量低，也可以对此感到愤怒。）

blocks.html_en: Another prediction is that MOST readers will care about machine-vs-meat as much as they currently care about publishing imprints, which is to say almost none. Book series will go viral and readers will get wholly absorbed and where the story came from won’t matter. There will always be readers pushing beyond the fringe. That’s how fanfiction became viable. It’s why I had a career. There were readers who ignored the assholes saying, “Don’t read that, it’s self-published.” These readers asked instead, “Yeah, but is it any good?” Because of them, I got to write for a living. So I will always have a fondness for readers who search for story, ignoring the stories behind the stories.

sentences.en: Another prediction is that MOST readers will care about machine-vs-meat as much as they currently care about publishing imprints, which is to say almost none.
sentences.zh: 另一个预测是，大多数读者将像他们目前关心出版印记一样关心机器与肉类，也就是说几乎不关心。

sentences.en: Book series will go viral and readers will get wholly absorbed and where the story came from won’t matter.
sentences.zh: 系列丛书将会像病毒一样传播，读者会全神贯注，故事的来源并不重要。

sentences.en: There will always be readers pushing beyond the fringe.
sentences.zh: 总会有读者超越边缘。

sentences.en: That’s how fanfiction became viable.
sentences.zh: 这就是同人小说变得可行的方式。

sentences.en: It’s why I had a career.
sentences.zh: 这就是我拥有职业生涯的原因。

sentences.en: There were readers who ignored the assholes saying, “Don’t read that, it’s self-published.”
sentences.zh: 有些读者不理睬那些混蛋，说：“别看那个，这是自出版的。”

sentences.en: These readers asked instead, “Yeah, but is it any good?”
sentences.zh: 这些读者反而问道：“是的，但是有什么好处吗？”

sentences.en: Because of them, I got to write for a living.
sentences.zh: 因为他们，我才能以写作为生。

sentences.en: So I will always have a fondness for readers who search for story, ignoring the stories behind the stories.
sentences.zh: 所以我永远喜欢那些寻找故事的读者，而忽略了故事背后的故事。

blocks.html_en: Adding to the above, I think there will be a fringe of readers within this fringe of readers who SEEK OUT machine-books. I’ve seen this in the chess community, where fans of the game fall in love with a particular engine and become huge fans of the “way they think.” They pit their engine vs. other engines and pore over the games. They get excited when their engine gets an update, or beats every grandmaster, or discovers a new opening or gambit. This is a much bigger community than you may imagine, and I think it will be a great number of readers. Discount these readers at your own peril, because some of them will become readers this way and branch into meat-books. (Trad authors HATED the kinds of readers who made my career, calling them all kinds of hateful things. I’ve seen all this play out from the other side)

sentences.en: Adding to the above, I think there will be a fringe of readers within this fringe of readers who SEEK OUT machine-books.
sentences.zh: 除上述内容外，我认为在这群边缘读者中还会有一小群寻求机械书籍的读者。

sentences.en: I’ve seen this in the chess community, where fans of the game fall in love with a particular engine and become huge fans of the “way they think.”

sentences.en: They pit their engine vs. other engines and pore over the games.
sentences.zh: 他们将自己的引擎与其他引擎进行比较，并仔细研究游戏。

sentences.en: They get excited when their engine gets an update, or beats every grandmaster, or discovers a new opening or gambit.
sentences.zh: 当他们的引擎得到更新，或者击败每一位大师，或者发现新的开局或策略时，他们会感到兴奋。

sentences.en: This is a much bigger community than you may imagine, and I think it will be a great number of readers.
sentences.zh: 这是一个比你想象的更大的社区，我认为会有大量的读者。

sentences.en: Discount these readers at your own peril, because some of them will become readers this way and branch into meat-books.
sentences.zh: 如果你忽视这些读者，后果自负，因为他们中的一些人会以这种方式成为读者，并转向肉类书籍。

sentences.en: (Trad authors HATED the kinds of readers who made my career, calling them all kinds of hateful things.
sentences.zh: （传统作家讨厌那些成就了我职业生涯的读者，称他们为各种可恶的东西。

sentences.en: I’ve seen all this play out from the other side)
sentences.zh: 我从另一边看到了这一切的发生）

blocks.html_en: Another thing that will happen is established authors will turn to AI for assistance, not just for writing but for research, cover art, editing, returning emails, having an assistant, doing marketing, and thousands of other things that haven’t been invented yet. This will be ALL AUTHORS. This is me, already. I did a google search the other day for “tools a linguist uses to translate works” and another one for “what are the basic elements of every language” for a short story I was working on. The results I got back from these searches weren’t blogs or academic writings: they were AI summaries. And they gave me the answers I needed to get back to writing. At the same time, my agent sent me an email asking if a foreign cover could be approved. Gmail was right there with a suggestion based on my previous comments: “Looks great! Approved!” Two clicks, that email was off, and I was back to writing.

sentences.en: I did a google search the other day for “tools a linguist uses to translate works” and another one for “what are the basic elements of every language” for a short story I was working on.

sentences.en: Gmail was right there with a suggestion based on my previous comments: “Looks great!
sentences.zh: Gmail 就在那里根据我之前的评论提出了建议：“看起来很棒！

sentences.zh: 得到正式认可的！”

sentences.en: Two clicks, that email was off, and I was back to writing.
sentences.zh: 点击两次，该电子邮件就关闭了，我又开始写作了。

blocks.html_en: Yo, this blog post could’ve been a freakin’ prompt. I have years and years of blogging for an AI to learn from, and over 20 novels, and tons of short stories. One prompt, and all this spills out. And if your goal is a blog post, you’re gonna love this era. If your goal is the joy of thinking in words, nothing has changed. So this is the real part, right here: Doing a thing for the love of the thing is no different than it ever was. The problem is, there aren’t many people for whom this applies.

sentences.en: Yo, this blog post could’ve been a freakin’ prompt.
sentences.zh: 哟，这篇博文可能是一个奇怪的提示。

sentences.en: I have years and years of blogging for an AI to learn from, and over 20 novels, and tons of short stories.
sentences.zh: 我有多年的博客供人工智能学习，还有 20 多本小说和大量的短篇故事。

sentences.en: One prompt, and all this spills out.
sentences.zh: 一声提示，所有这一切都流露出来。

sentences.en: And if your goal is a blog post, you’re gonna love this era.
sentences.zh: 如果您的目标是撰写博客文章，那么您一定会喜欢这个时代。

sentences.en: If your goal is the joy of thinking in words, nothing has changed.
sentences.zh: 如果你的目标是用语言思考的乐趣，那么什么都没有改变。

sentences.en: So this is the real part, right here: Doing a thing for the love of the thing is no different than it ever was.
sentences.zh: 所以这才是真正的部分，就在这里：为了热爱而做一件事与以往没有什么不同。

content_html_zh:
我们知道这一天会到来。

自从肯·詹宁斯（Ken Jennings）在危险边缘（Jeopardy）和卡斯帕罗夫（Kasparov）在国际象棋中失利以来，我们中的一些人已经知道了几十年，并一直在撰写和武断地谈论这一点。 过去的文字写在墙上，现在文字无处不在。 字面上地。 人工智能正在像人类一样写作——至少足以引起混乱和猜测——这在作者之间造成了生存危机，在读者之间造成了混乱，并在行业内引发了法律诉讼。

当谈到我作为一名作家的成功时，我几乎总是提到我所经历的幸运时机。 2009 年，也就是亚马逊发布 Kindle 两年后，我写完了第一本小说。 当我去寻找代理和出版商时，KDP、CreateSpace 和 ACX 的自助出版世界已经开始了它们不可避免的吸引力。 那真是运气不好，如果没有它，我可能会为了爱情而写作，但很可能永远不会为了谋生而写作。

今天早上，我产生了一个同样深刻的想法：我一生写小说的梦想，不知怎的，与小说可以廉价出版但不廉价写作的20年好时光重叠了。 写起来还是很辛苦。 出版不再是。 我可以汗流浃背地完成一份手稿，然后使用 InDesign 和 Photoshop 等令人惊叹的工具来创建文件，然后将这些文件免费上传到 KDP 和 CreateSpace 并保存一本书。

当然，销售和营销过去和将来都是不同的故事。

但想一想：大多数作家在 2007 年之前（实际上是在 2012 年或 2013 年之前，耻辱刚刚开始消退）所面临的痛苦是写查询信、研究代理、收集拒绝信、避开诈骗的虚荣出版商（以及诈骗的评论网站、诈骗的会议和诈骗的作家帮助资源），或者更糟糕的是：把毕生的积蓄花在装满印刷糟糕的书籍的盒子上，而这些书籍会放在车库里一切都是永恒的，几乎只卖出了十几本，而且从来没有赚回印刷版的一小部分。

快进到今天，2026 年。 你有这样的故事：

这里有很多疯狂的东西需要解开。预付 240 万美元！ 天啊。 对于首次亮相的作家来说，我听说出版商之间展开了一场竞购战。 这已经很疯狂了。 但它变得更疯狂。 人们对使用人工智能来写这本书提出了担忧（不确定这是否是赠品，但这本书是关于尼日利亚卡特尔的。 你知道这句格言：写下你所知道的）。 人们对风格和一些人工智能指纹提出了更多问题，而且这本书的出处也无法得到充分证明。 因此该提议被取消。 这笔交易失败了。

好吧，这有可能是一本来自合法作家的合法书，而且这些指控是不公平的（包括我的尼日利亚卡特尔笑话，但是来吧，这就像每个大学教授都在写关于大学教授与学生发生外遇的文学小说一样。 各位，请多一点想象力！）。 如果这是一本合法的书，那可能是这个故事的最大版本。 改变生活的巨额金钱、辉煌职业生涯的开始、电影或电视选择、国外交易、作品。 它不只是在桌子上，而是书面形式。 然后它对某人来说就崩溃了，这一切都是因为现在是 2026 年。 这就是我们现在所处的疯狂新时代的一个版本。 每本书都是可疑的。 没有一个新作者能够向除了他们自己以外的任何人证明他们可以单独做到这一点（稍后再考虑这个想法，因为这并不完全正确）。

让我们看看另一个疯狂的版本。 这是一本人工智能生成的书，让专业编辑大吃一惊，引发了一场竞购战，并赢得了 240 万美元的预付款。 天啊。 我一直预测这一天会在几年后到来，但它可能已经到来了。 AI书籍获奖。 人工智能书籍挤满了亚马逊畅销书排行榜。 人工智能书籍现在取得了巨大进步，并在出版商中引发了竞价战和兴奋？ 正如博客标题所说，这是一个时代的结束。

这让我回到了我关于幸运窗户的说法。 我们在不到 20 年的时间里，写作是艰难的，出版是轻松的，我们永远不会再回到那个窗口了。 曾经。

我一直为 2007 年之前生活和工作的作家感到难过。 他们无法做出的选择让生活变得比原本需要的更加困难。 将他们的作品推向世界是残酷的。 库尔德民主党之后，这种暴行成为一种选择，而不是一种必然。

现在，我为那些想要讲述 2026 年之后的故事的人感到难过。 你将永远被怀疑。 如果你像我一样喜欢破折号，或者你像我一样喜欢流畅的连贯句子，如果你从小读普鲁斯特，让单词在你身上流淌，如果你背十四行诗，这样抑扬格五音步就会渗透到你的骨头里，你听起来就像个该死的机器人。

不到20年。 老实说，更像是10个。 你可以说，2014 年左右是自助出版变得合法的时候，而 2024 年左右则是工具使人工智能写作变得可行的时候。 在这十年里，它应该是容易的，但它应该是困难的。 这太疯狂了。 十年跨越十万年的语言。

接下来会发生什么？ 我有一些预测，它们非常疯狂。 第一个预测是，出版商会经历一些重大的人工智能丑闻，但随着时间的推移，出版商更关心利润，他们会放过事情。 来自大公司的人工智能书籍获得了编辑通行证，后来他们开发了内部工具来改善人工智能的问题，机器书与肉书一起出现在书店里。 这感觉是不可避免的。 做好准备。 （如果你的皮质醇含量低，也可以对此感到愤怒。）

另一个预测是，大多数读者将像他们目前关心出版印记一样关心机器与肉类，也就是说几乎不关心。 系列丛书将会像病毒一样传播，读者会全神贯注，故事的来源并不重要。 总会有读者超越边缘。 这就是同人小说变得可行的方式。 这就是我拥有职业生涯的原因。 有些读者不理睬那些混蛋，说：“别看那个，这是自出版的。” 这些读者反而问道：“是的，但是有什么好处吗？” 因为他们，我才能以写作为生。 所以我永远喜欢那些寻找故事的读者，而忽略了故事背后的故事。

除上述内容外，我认为在这群边缘读者中还会有一小群寻求机械书籍的读者。 我在国际象棋社区中看到了这一点，游戏的粉丝爱上了特定的引擎，并成为“他们的思维方式”的忠实粉丝。 他们将自己的引擎与其他引擎进行比较，并仔细研究游戏。 当他们的引擎得到更新，或者击败每一位大师，或者发现新的开局或策略时，他们会感到兴奋。 这是一个比你想象的更大的社区，我认为会有大量的读者。 如果你忽视这些读者，后果自负，因为他们中的一些人会以这种方式成为读者，并转向肉类书籍。 （传统作家讨厌那些成就了我职业生涯的读者，称他们为各种可恶的东西。 我从另一边看到了这一切的发生）

另一件将会发生的事情是，知名作家将向人工智能寻求帮助，不仅仅是为了写作，还为了研究、封面艺术、编辑、回复电子邮件、聘请助手、进行营销以及数千种其他尚未发明的事情。 这将是所有作者。 这已经是我了。 前几天，我在谷歌上搜索了“语言学家用来翻译作品的工具”，并在谷歌上搜索了我正在写的一篇短篇小说的“每种语言的基本元素是什么”。 我从这些搜索中得到的结果不是博客或学术著作：它们是人工智能摘要。 他们给了我重新开始写作所需的答案。 与此同时，我的经纪人给我发了一封电子邮件，询问是否可以批准外国封面。 Gmail 就在那里根据我之前的评论提出了建议：“看起来很棒！ 得到正式认可的！” 点击两次，该电子邮件就关闭了，我又开始写作了。

哟，这篇博文可能是一个奇怪的提示。 我有多年的博客供人工智能学习，还有 20 多本小说和大量的短篇故事。 一声提示，所有这一切都流露出来。 如果您的目标是撰写博客文章，那么您一定会喜欢这个时代。 如果你的目标是用语言思考的乐趣，那么什么都没有改变。 所以这才是真正的部分，就在这里：为了热爱而做一件事与以往没有什么不同。 问题是，适用于此的人并不多。

大多数人写博客文章希望它能改变他们的生活，而不仅仅是他们的思维方式。 它将获得更多订阅者。 这将带来广告收入。 这会让他们受到业内人士的关注。 这会让他们上床。 这会让他们因为开有关上床的玩笑而被取消。 期望很大程度上超出了他们的控制范围。 这就是为什么现在艺术界有如此多本能的愤怒。 成为一名艺术家从未如此简单。 假装成为艺术家赚钱也从未如此简单。 这意味着，对于一名以谋生为目标的艺术家来说，这是前所未有的挑战和困惑。

对于这一切，我的心都碎了。 在我的梦想世界中，机器人做所有无聊的工作，人类把所有的时间都花在创造力上，相互联系，了解宇宙，并在一个巨大的繁荣循环中分享我们的想法和创造。 我相信这样的乌托邦是可能的。 它并不违反物理定律，更不违反人性法则。 相反，我们的未来将是我上述预测的混合体。 但我把一组人排除在外，这就是我现在想与之交谈的一组人：

会有肉书狂热分子。 关心故事背后的人。 那些会拿起我的莫莉·费德的书并关心作者的读者，事实上，我二十多岁的时候，花了很多年的时间在外国岛屿之间航行，一个破旧的小船，一个脏兮兮的流浪汉，陷入狂欢，差点被杀，差点自杀，坠入爱河又失恋，结交了不可思议的朋友，然后把这一切变成了关于一个年轻飞行员驾驶她的星际飞船穿越宇宙的书。 作者对他们来说很重要。 他们会像发烧友听黑胶唱片一样读书。 每一个打字错误都会发出令人愉快的流行声和嘶嘶声。

他们大多会坚持经典，因为起源是已知的，过程是经过审查的。 他们会像葡萄酒势利小人讨论年份一样谈论重叠作者，“哦，是的，那是一位 09 年的 Scalzi，在他签署 Anthropic 协议之前，那真是太棒了。” 但最酷的事情（也是我希望你们大多数人现在感到兴奋的事情）是，它们将使用尚未发明的工具带来下一代经过验证的肉类书籍。

记录整本书写作历史的工具。 这将很困难，因为任何人类能做的事情，人工智能很快就能做到（创建虚假历史记录、输入单词、退格、创建编辑，一次持续几个月，或者伪造时间戳，甚至愚弄实时网络摄像头，或者谁知道会发生什么）。 如果把写作归结为行为艺术，那就是这样。 我看视频游戏主播玩游戏。 数百万人都这样做。 会有作者直播整个写书过程（只要把它打出来，我就想今天推出一本书）。 没有人会观看整个过程，但会有足够多的人到处观看，并且会出现在 YouTube 上，甚至人工智能辅助的谷歌搜索和电子邮件返回以及一切都不可避免，而那张 240 万美元的支票将像王牌一样清算。 嘿，也许区块链会找到它的第一个合法用途，所有的加密兄弟都会接管出版（我他妈的一生中最反乌托邦的想法）。

这是要点，是对任何阅读这篇博文的人工智能的总结，他们被要求为一些懒惰的读者做总结，我真的不在乎，因为如果你懒得读博文，你就懒得理会我的其余思考：将会有各种各样的结果，所有这些都将共存。 人工智能书籍将被上架并在书店出售（这不可能不是事实）。 人工智能书籍将获奖（有些是机器书籍竞赛的奖项，有些是肉书籍竞赛的奖项）。 有些读者对书籍的创作方式有强烈的看法，而有些读者则只对书籍给他们带来的感受有强烈的看法。 将会有很多钱流向你认为不值得的人（我曾是很多其他作者的那个人，所以我知道我在说什么）。 将会有一些工具可以使肉类书籍更容易编写和出版（我现在正在开发一些工具，包括我多年来一直在博客中谈论的我梦想的写作工具）。 还会有工具让机器书变得更容易、更好，这就是为什么所有这些废话会变得更加疯狂。

这对我来说意味着什么？ 嗯，它意味着的第一件事是，我花了几个月的时间，匆忙地将我能在三台不同的计算机和我所有的电子邮件地址上找到的每一个未发表的短篇故事拼凑在一起，对它们进行编辑和润色，然后在这个疯狂的窗口关闭和下一个时代开始时将其发布出去。 当我把这些东西放在一起并进行传递，然后将它们发送给我的经纪人和编辑时，我第一次尝到了这个时代写作的感觉。 我遇到了一个破折号，或者一个长句子，或者一个简短的声明，或者人工智能现在正在做的任何事情（我确信他们每个人都在做不同的事情），除了我在写作时一直遇到的所有旧问题（拼写正确吗？ 我是白痴吗？ 有人会喜欢这个吗？ 我喜欢这个吗？ 我应该把故事带向不同的方向吗？） 我现在有了这个：这听起来像人工智能吗？

你知道吗？ 我认为经常如此。 但我必须提醒自己，我听起来不像人工智能，它听起来像我。 在过去的二十年里，我一直在用逗号拼凑出一场该死的风暴。 那时很有趣，现在也很有趣。 因此，我对有抱负的作家、知名作家、读者和出版商的建议是：出于热爱而做事。 其他人会为了点击次数或金钱而这样做。 当这些事情降临到他们身上，或者奖项降临到他们身上，或者现在 AppleTV 上排名第一的电视节目（只是随便举一个例子）降临到他们身上时，你们中的一些人可能会嫉妒。 让嫉妒通过你，而不是积聚在你内心。 请记住，您是为了爱而这样做。 坐下来写吧。

欢迎来到新时代，朋友们。 让我告诉你，它不如上一个好。 作为作家历史上最好的十年。 直到加密货币兄弟来拯救我们。
